case_analysis.focal_point: Whether restitution imposed under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act is a criminal punishment such that retroactive changes to MVRA restitution rules trigger the Ex Post Facto Clause.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 (Ex Post Facto Clause) and the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (MVRA), primarily 18 U.S.C. § 3663A and related enforcement/collection provisions.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that MVRA restitution is part of the defendant’s criminal sentence and functions as a penal sanction (mandatory, imposed at sentencing, tied to conviction and supervised-release consequences, enforced with criminal-justice tools). Because it is punishment, Congress cannot retroactively apply MVRA amendments that worsen the defendant’s position (e.g., expand enforcement/collection time or otherwise make the restitution obligation more onerous) without violating the Ex Post Facto Clause. Petitioner also emphasizes that calling restitution “civil” or purely compensatory ignores how MVRA restitution operates in practice and risks destabilizing settled constitutional doctrines (including the circuit consensus treating restitution as criminal for Seventh Amendment purposes).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government initially opposed certiorari but, after cert was granted, notified the Court it would not defend the Eighth Circuit’s rationale and would support petitioner on the question presented. In the oral-argument excerpts, the government position is: (1) restitution under the MVRA should be treated as criminal punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes, but (2) not every retroactive MVRA change necessarily increases punishment; specifically, the government sought to preserve on remand an argument that extending the time to collect restitution does not increase the defendant’s punishment (i.e., it may be a procedural/collection mechanism rather than an increase in the penal sanction). Because the United States is no longer defending the judgment below, a court-appointed amicus (John F. Bash) argued to affirm: restitution is primarily remedial/compensatory rather than punitive, and under the Court’s punitive-versus-remedial framework it should not be treated as criminal punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes; he also raised concerns that deeming restitution ‘civil’ would create Seventh Amendment and possibly Sixth Amendment complications, though he maintained MVRA restitution is more remedial than punitive.
key_precedents: Feltner v. Columbia Pictures Television, Inc.

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that MVRA restitution is primarily remedial and thus outside Ex Post Facto scrutiny—still runs into Ward/Hudson’s threshold focus on Congress’s intent as revealed by statutory design. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, the MVRA makes restitution mandatory “when sentencing a defendant,” routes it through Rule 32 and § 3664 procedures, and embeds it in the criminal judgment—signals that are difficult to reconcile with a purely civil, compensatory scheme absent the “clearest proof” to the contrary. Justice Barrett’s citation to Pasquantino (and Paroline) strengthens our footing by confirming that our own precedents recognize restitution can “serve punitive purposes” even while compensating victims, undercutting any categorical nonpunitive label. Consistent with minimalism and to avoid unnecessary spillover, I would hold only that MVRA restitution is punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes and leave to remand whether the retroactive collection-time change increases punishment in operation under Weaver/Collins.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that restitution is “primarily remedial” and thus outside the Ex Post Facto Clause—fails under an original public meaning approach because the relevant question is whether the legal consequence is attached to the criminal judgment upon conviction as part of the sentence. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, the MVRA mandates restitution “when sentencing a defendant,” embeds it in the criminal judgment, and enforces it through criminal-judgment mechanisms, which are strong textual and structural indicators of punishment rather than a freestanding civil debt. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Pasquantino (and related cases like Paroline) matters because it confirms this Court has already recognized restitution can “mete out” criminal punishment even while benefiting victims, undercutting any categorical nonpunitive label. Whether a specific retroactive amendment increases punishment in operation is a separate Weaver/Collins application question for remand, not a basis to deny that MVRA restitution is punishment for ex post facto purposes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that MVRA restitution is “primarily remedial” and thus civil—does not overcome the statute’s text and structure: Congress required restitution “when sentencing a defendant,” made it mandatory, and embedded it in the criminal judgment with criminal enforcement tools, which under Ward/Hudson is powerful evidence of punitive design absent the “clearest proof” to the contrary. Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on statutory placement and sentencing integration is decisive for a textualist analysis: this is not a freestanding civil cause of action but a consequence annexed to conviction. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline matters because those cases recognize restitution can “mete out” punishment and “serve punitive purposes,” foreclosing the Eighth Circuit’s categorical nonpunitive label even if victims benefit. I would keep the holding narrow and, as Justice Kagan suggests, leave the separate Weaver/Collins question—whether the retroactive collection-time extension increases punishment in practical effect—for remand.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that MVRA restitution is chiefly compensatory and should be treated like a civil debt—does not overcome the statutory design signals that it is imposed “when sentencing” upon conviction and integrated into the criminal judgment. Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on Ward/Hudson’s intent-first framework is persuasive: Congress chose criminal procedures and enforcement tools that can constrain liberty, which matters most for indigent defendants and makes the sanction meaningfully different from ordinary civil collection. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline further undercuts any categorical “nonpunitive” label by recognizing restitution can simultaneously compensate and serve punitive purposes. I therefore continue to reject the Eighth Circuit’s categorical rule, while agreeing with colleagues (e.g., Justice Kagan) that whether this specific retroactive collection-extension increases punishment can be assessed on remand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that restitution is victim-directed compensation and therefore more like civil debt enforcement—still doesn’t overcome Ward/Hudson’s focus on Congress’s design and the “clearest proof” requirement. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the MVRA text imposes restitution “when sentencing a defendant,” integrates it into the criminal judgment, and routes it through Rule 32 and § 3664 procedures—structural and procedural markers that read as criminal sanctioning even if victims benefit. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline is important for my analysis because it rejects a categorical either/or: restitution can be compensatory in effect while also serving punitive purposes, which makes the Eighth Circuit’s blanket ‘nonpunitive’ label untenable. I would keep the holding narrow—restitution counts as punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes—while leaving for remand the distinct Weaver/Collins question whether this particular retroactive collection change increases punishment in operation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument remains that MVRA restitution is “primarily remedial” and thus outside the Ex Post Facto Clause, but Ward and Hudson direct us to start with Congress’s design, and the MVRA by its terms applies “when sentencing a defendant” and is entered in the criminal judgment—features that ordinarily mark punishment. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on statutory placement and integration into Rule 32/§ 3664 criminal procedures reinforces that Congress chose a penal mechanism, and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline confirms our cases recognize restitution may compensate victims yet still “serve punitive purposes.” Even if certain amendments (like collection-time extensions) might be characterized as procedural in some applications, that is a distinct Weaver/Collins inquiry about whether the retroactive change increases punishment, not a basis for the Eighth Circuit’s categorical rule that MVRA restitution is never punishment. Nothing raised by colleagues supplies the “clearest proof” needed to override the statute’s text and structure under the Ward/Hudson framework.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that MVRA restitution is primarily compensatory and thus civil—does not overcome the Ward/Hudson threshold inquiry into Congress’s design: as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Congress placed restitution in Title 18, made it mandatory “when sentencing a defendant,” and integrated it into the criminal judgment and Rule 32 procedures, all classic indicia of a penal sanction absent the “clearest proof” to the contrary. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline matters because those cases recognize restitution’s punitive aims alongside compensation, making the Eighth Circuit’s categorical “never punishment” rule untenable under our precedent and tradition. I agree with colleagues that we should write narrowly and remand on the separate Weaver/Collins question whether the specific retroactive amendment increases punishment in operation. No argument presented undermines my institutionalist view that we should adhere to the statute’s structure and our existing descriptions of restitution’s mixed—but undeniably penal—character.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that restitution is compensatory and therefore not “punishment”—does not overcome the MVRA’s text and structure, which make restitution mandatory “when sentencing a defendant” and “in addition to … any other penalty,” strongly signaling a criminal sanction absent the “clearest proof” otherwise under Ward/Hudson. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on statutory placement within the sentencing judgment and its administration through criminal procedures reinforces that Congress treated restitution as part of the criminal sentence, not a freestanding civil remedy. The compensatory features do not negate punishment where, as I noted and Justice Kagan echoed, our precedents (including Pasquantino and Paroline) recognize restitution can serve punitive purposes while also compensating victims. I remain persuaded we can hold MVRA restitution is punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes while leaving for remand, as several colleagues urge, whether this particular retroactive collection-time extension increases punishment in operation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that MVRA restitution is compensatory and retroactive enforcement tweaks are merely remedial—does not overcome Ward/Hudson’s starting presumption that Congress’s design controls absent the “clearest proof.” As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the MVRA makes restitution mandatory “when sentencing a defendant,” embeds it in the criminal judgment, and deploys criminal-justice enforcement tools, which in practical consequence operate as a coercive penal burden rather than an ordinary civil debt. Justice Sotomayor’s focus on the real-world supervision and revocation leverage underscores why treating this as purely civil would let retroactive increases in sentencing burdens evade Ex Post Facto scrutiny. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Pasquantino (and Paroline) further confirms our precedents already recognize restitution’s punitive purposes alongside compensation, supporting a narrow holding that MVRA restitution qualifies as “punishment,” while leaving the separate ‘increase in punishment’ inquiry for remand.

John Roberts.reasoning: The MVRA operates as part of the criminal sentencing scheme: it is imposed at sentencing upon conviction, is mandatory for covered offenses, and is enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms (18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664), all strong indicia that Congress treated the obligation as penal for Ex Post Facto purposes. Under Hudson v. United States and Ward, the threshold inquiry is legislative intent; here the placement, procedure, and mandatory nature of MVRA restitution show a preference for criminal treatment, making retroactive, punishment-increasing changes subject to Art. I, § 9, cl. 3. This conclusion can be reached narrowly without deciding whether any particular retroactive collection extension necessarily increases punishment, leaving that question for remand. The Eighth Circuit’s contrary reasoning is difficult to square with this Court’s repeated description of restitution as a component of the criminal sentence in cases like Dolan v. United States.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause forbids retroactive laws that “inflict[] a greater punishment, than the law annexed to the crime, when committed,” Calder v. Bull, and that original meaning turns on whether the consequence is imposed as part of the criminal judgment. Under the MVRA, restitution is mandatory “when sentencing a defendant” for specified crimes, 18 U.S.C. § 3663A(a)(1), and is enforced through the criminal process (including conditions of supervised release and revocation consequences), which confirms it operates as a penal sanction attached to conviction rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Whatever its compensatory benefits, restitution under this statute is imposed by the sentencing court as part of the criminal sentence, so retroactive amendments that make that obligation more onerous fall within the Ex Post Facto Clause’s prohibition (subject to the separate question whether a particular change actually increases punishment under Weaver v. Graham/Collins v. Youngblood). To the extent contrary lower-court reasoning treats MVRA restitution as categorically nonpunitive, it departs from the constitutional text as originally understood and should not be preserved by precedent alone.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The MVRA’s text and structure treat restitution as part of the criminal sentence: it is mandatory upon conviction, imposed at sentencing under criminal rules (18 U.S.C. § 3664(c); Fed. R. Crim. P. 32), and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, all of which strongly indicate punishment rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Under the Ward/Hudson/Ursery framework, Congress’s use of classic criminal procedures is powerful evidence the sanction is criminal, and the Court has likewise described MVRA restitution as imposed through the "manifest procedural differences" of criminal sentencing rather than civil litigation. Paroline and Dolan may call restitution “primarily remedial,” but that purpose does not override Congress’s decision to make restitution a mandatory penal consequence of conviction; treating it as nonpunitive would invite serious doctrinal disruption (including the uniform circuit treatment in the Seventh Amendment context) and would weaken the Ex Post Facto Clause’s protection against retroactive increases in penal burdens. The proper disposition is to hold MVRA restitution is punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes and leave for remand whether a particular retroactive collection amendment actually increases the punishment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: MVRA restitution is imposed at sentencing “in addition to … any other penalty” for a criminal conviction, 18 U.S.C. § 3663A(a)(1), and is enforced through the criminal-justice system, making it part of the criminal sentence rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Under Hudson v. United States (quoting Ward), the ex post facto inquiry begins with statutory construction and Congress’s evident intent; here Congress located restitution in the criminal code and tethered it to conviction and supervised-release consequences, so it is properly treated as punishment for Ex Post Facto Clause purposes. Treating MVRA restitution as nonpunitive would also ignore its real-world coercive effects on defendants—including indigent defendants—who face continued criminal-justice supervision and sanctions if they cannot pay, while destabilizing settled practice recognizing restitution’s criminal character (cf. Dolan v. United States; Paroline v. United States). Because restitution is punishment, retroactive changes that make the obligation more onerous can trigger the Ex Post Facto Clause, even if particular collection extensions may require a separate “increased punishment” analysis on remand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: MVRA restitution is imposed by the sentencing court as part of the criminal judgment, using criminal sentencing procedures Congress expressly specified in 18 U.S.C. § 3664(c) (incorporating Fed. R. Crim. P. 32), and it attaches to conviction with enforcement mechanisms integrated into the criminal process—features that, under Hudson v. United States and the Ward/Ursery line, strongly indicate a criminal sanction rather than a distinct civil remedy. Our cases also describe MVRA restitution as a component of the criminal sentencing framework even while recognizing its compensatory aim; Paroline v. United States emphasized the “manifest procedural differences” between restitution at sentencing and civil tort suits, and Dolan v. United States treated restitution as a penal consequence administered through sentencing. Because it functions as punishment in operation and placement within the sentencing scheme, retroactive MVRA changes that make the defendant’s position worse can trigger the Ex Post Facto Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3), though whether a particular collection-time extension increases punishment can be addressed on remand. Treating MVRA restitution as nonpunitive would also create serious doctrinal instability given how uniformly lower courts have treated restitution as criminal for related constitutional inquiries.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The MVRA’s text and structure place restitution within the criminal sentencing system: it is imposed only “when sentencing a defendant convicted” of specified offenses, 18 U.S.C. § 3663A(a)(1), and administered under criminal-sentencing procedures, § 3664(c), indicating Congress chose a criminal sanction rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Under Ward and Hudson, whether the Ex Post Facto Clause applies is “at least initially” a matter of statutory construction, and here Congress’s choice to embed restitution in the criminal judgment—backed by the coercive machinery of criminal enforcement—answers that question. That restitution has compensatory features does not strip its penal character when, as Dolan and Paroline recognize, it operates as a mandatory component of the sentence imposed because of a conviction. Accordingly, retroactive changes that make the restitution obligation more onerous can trigger the Ex Post Facto Clause, leaving for remand the separate question whether a particular collection-extension is merely procedural or instead increases punishment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The MVRA’s restitution scheme is imposed by the sentencing court as part of the criminal judgment and is governed by criminal sentencing procedures, see 18 U.S.C. § 3664(c), making it a penal consequence of conviction rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Under Hudson v. United States and Ward, the threshold inquiry is Congress’s intent, and here the MVRA’s text, placement in Title 18, and mandatory imposition at sentencing indicate Congress created a criminal sanction subject to the Ex Post Facto Clause. Our restitution cases likewise describe restitution as a component of the criminal sentence and administered through sentencing mechanisms, see Dolan v. United States and Paroline v. United States, which supports treating it as punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes. The extent to which a particular retroactive amendment “increases” punishment (e.g., collection time) can be assessed on remand, but the Eighth Circuit’s categorical conclusion that MVRA restitution is not punishment is inconsistent with the statute’s structure and this Court’s framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The MVRA’s text and operation treat restitution as part of the criminal sentence: it is imposed “in addition to … any other penalty” at sentencing upon conviction, 18 U.S.C. § 3663A(a)(1), and is enforced through the criminal-judgment machinery, indicating a penal sanction rather than a freestanding civil remedy. This Court has repeatedly characterized federal criminal restitution as serving punitive ends—most directly in Pasquantino v. United States (MVRA restitution “mete[s] out appropriate criminal punishment”) and Paroline v. United States (restitution “serves punitive purposes”)—which aligns with the Mendoza-Martinez/Hudson/Ward focus on effects and function, not labels. Given that restitution is criminal punishment, retroactive MVRA changes that make the restitution obligation more onerous can trigger the Ex Post Facto Clause, leaving for remand the separate question whether particular collection-time extensions merely alter enforcement procedure rather than increasing punishment. Treating MVRA restitution as nonpunitive would also sit uneasily with the settled understanding that restitution is imposed as part of the criminal case and sentence (see Dolan v. United States), and would invite destabilizing cross-constitutional consequences.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Hudson v. United States and Ward, the Ex Post Facto analysis begins with Congress’s intent and permits departure only upon the “clearest proof” that a nominally civil sanction is in purpose or effect punitive. Here, Congress embedded MVRA restitution in the criminal sentencing process—mandated at sentencing upon conviction, governed by criminal sentencing procedures (18 U.S.C. § 3664(c)), and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms—features that align restitution with a penal sanction rather than a freestanding civil remedy, consistent with the Court’s recognition in Paroline and Dolan that restitution operates as part of the criminal case even if it has compensatory aims. Treating MVRA restitution as nonpunitive would undermine procedural fairness by allowing retroactive increases in the practical burdens of a sentence without Ex Post Facto scrutiny, and would create instability with the uniform circuit treatment of restitution as criminal for Seventh Amendment purposes (cf. Feltner, Tull). Accordingly, restitution under the MVRA is “punishment” for Ex Post Facto purposes, though on remand the lower court may still assess whether a particular retroactive amendment actually increases punishment.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether restitution imposed under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act is a criminal punishment such that retroactive application triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 (Ex Post Facto Clause) as applied to restitution ordered under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (MVRA), 18 U.S.C. § 3663A and related enforcement provisions.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues MVRA restitution is a penal component of a criminal sentence: it is imposed only upon conviction, is mandatory and court-ordered at sentencing, is backed by criminal enforcement mechanisms, and serves traditional penal aims (retribution, deterrence, rehabilitation) in addition to victim compensation. Because it functions as punishment, Congress cannot retroactively apply MVRA provisions that disadvantage defendants without violating the Ex Post Facto Clause. Petitioner and supporting amici also stress that calling MVRA restitution 'civil' would create serious structural problems (e.g., Seventh Amendment jury-trial implications) and conflict with how courts have long treated restitution as part of criminal sentencing.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government (post-cert grant) no longer defends the Eighth Circuit’s rationale and supports vacatur; it aligns with petitioner on the narrow question presented that MVRA restitution is 'criminal punishment' for Ex Post Facto purposes, while seeking to preserve arguments on remand that the particular retroactive change at issue may not 'increase punishment' (e.g., extending collection/enforcement time may be characterized as nonpunitive or not materially increasing the penalty). A court-appointed amicus defending the judgment below argues restitution is primarily remedial/compensatory—more like tort compensation than punishment—citing Supreme Court language that restitution’s 'primary purpose' is remedial; under a 'more remedial than punitive' framework, it should not be treated as punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes. That amicus also flags potential vehicle/DIG concerns and warns that treating restitution as civil could destabilize Sixth/Seventh Amendment doctrine, even while using remedial-purpose cases to defend the Eighth Circuit’s outcome.
key_precedents: Feltner v. Columbia Pictures Television, Inc.

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—pressed in Dolan and Paroline—that restitution is “primarily remedial” does not answer Hudson/Smith’s threshold inquiry into Congress’s design: under the MVRA, restitution is mandatory, conviction-triggered, imposed “when sentencing” and “in addition to … any other penalty,” and enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms, all of which are strong indicia of punishment even if victim compensation is a central aim. Justice Barrett’s emphasis that Hudson starts with statutory construction reinforces my minimalist approach: we can hold only that MVRA restitution counts as “punishment” for Ex Post Facto purposes without deciding broader questions about every restitution regime. Justice Alito’s concern about spillover into Apprendi/Seventh Amendment territory confirms the need for a narrow, statute-specific classification and a remand on whether the retroactive change actually increases punishment under Weaver. Nothing in colleagues’ cited precedents undermines that limited holding, because Dolan/Paroline’s “primary purpose” language coexists with their repeated characterization of restitution as part of the criminal sentencing process.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent claim—that restitution is merely compensatory and thus outside the Ex Post Facto Clause—cannot overcome the MVRA’s text making restitution a conviction-triggered sanction imposed “when sentencing” and “in addition to … any other penalty,” which is the language and architecture of punishment as originally understood. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about Congress embedding restitution in the criminal judgment and enforcing it through criminal-judgment mechanisms confirms, under Hudson/Smith’s intent-and-effects framework, that this operates as penal law even if it has remedial benefits. Dolan and Paroline’s statements about “primary purpose” do not control a textualist analysis of the operative statutory command; at most they show restitution may be both compensatory and punitive. I therefore agree with Justice Barrett that statutory design is dispositive here, while leaving for remand whether the retroactive change actually increases punishment under Weaver.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The best respondent argument remains that MVRA restitution is “primarily remedial” (as Dolan and Paroline say) and so should be treated as civil, but that label cannot overcome Congress’s design choices: § 3663A orders restitution only “when sentencing a defendant convicted” and “in addition to … any other penalty,” which is the architecture of criminal punishment, not a freestanding civil damages remedy. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about the conviction-triggered, mandatory, court-ordered deprivation enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms fits Hudson/Smith’s intent-and-effects framework and shows sufficiently punitive form and operation even if victims are compensated. Justice Barrett’s emphasis that Hudson starts with statutory construction strengthens the narrow, statute-specific holding here: we should not recharacterize a sanction embedded in the criminal sentence as “civil” in a way that would generate serious practical and structural anomalies. I therefore remain with Petitioner, with remand appropriate on whether the particular retroactive change increased the penalty under Weaver.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that restitution is “primarily remedial” because it compensates victims (Dolan; Paroline)—still doesn’t answer how the MVRA actually operates against defendants: it is mandatory, triggered only upon conviction, imposed “when sentencing,” labeled “in addition to … any other penalty,” and enforced through criminal-judgment machinery, which makes its real-world effect meaningfully punitive for Ex Post Facto purposes. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on those sentencing-embedded features is persuasive because, under Smith v. Doe’s intent-and-effects framework, compensatory aims do not negate punitive form and effects when the sanction is administered as part of the criminal sentence. Justice Kagan’s Hudson point strengthens the analysis: statutory design comes first, and Congress deliberately placed restitution in the criminal sentencing scheme rather than creating a civil damages action, so recharacterizing it as “civil” would create workability and fairness problems (including the Seventh Amendment tensions Roberts flags) that particularly burden indigent defendants. I would therefore classify MVRA restitution as “punishment” for Ex Post Facto analysis while leaving the distinct Weaver question—whether the retroactive change actually increases punishment—open for remand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that MVRA restitution is purely remedial and thus outside the Ex Post Facto Clause—doesn’t survive Hudson’s threshold focus on legislative design: Congress required restitution “when sentencing a defendant convicted” and expressly made it “in addition to … any other penalty,” which textually situates it inside the criminal sentence even if it compensates victims. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the MVRA’s integration into the criminal judgment and its criminal enforcement mechanisms is persuasive under the Smith v. Doe intent-and-effects framework, because those features are difficult to reconcile with a genuinely civil label absent the “clearest proof” to the contrary. Dolan and Paroline’s “primary purpose” language (which several colleagues cite) affects my analysis only to the extent it confirms restitution’s compensatory aim; it does not negate that this conviction-triggered, sentencing-imposed obligation functions as punishment for Ex Post Facto classification. I agree with Justice Barrett that the narrow, workable path is to treat MVRA restitution as punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes while leaving the separate Weaver question—whether the retroactive change actually increases punishment—for remand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that restitution is often described as “primarily compensatory” (Dolan; Paroline), but under Hudson’s sequencing—emphasized by Justice Barrett—we start with Congress’s design, and the MVRA’s text attaches restitution only upon conviction and commands it be ordered “when sentencing” and “in addition to … any other penalty,” which is the language and architecture of criminal punishment. Chief Justice Roberts is right that relabeling this sentencing component as “civil” would generate serious structural anomalies (including Seventh Amendment and broader sentencing coherence concerns), which is a strong signal that the statute’s operation is penal even if it has remedial aims. Under Smith v. Doe’s intent-and-effects framework, the conviction-triggered, mandatory, judgment-integrated character of MVRA restitution supplies the “punitive” markers, and the compensatory purpose does not supply the “clearest proof” needed to overcome that. I would keep the holding narrow—MVRA restitution counts as punishment for Ex Post Facto classification—while leaving for remand whether the retroactive change actually increases punishment under Weaver, consistent with Justice Roberts’s proposed course.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The best respondent argument remains Dolan/Paroline’s description of restitution as “primarily remedial,” but that characterization cannot trump Congress’s design choices: the MVRA makes restitution mandatory, conviction-triggered, and imposed by the sentencing court “in addition to … any other penalty,” which is classic penal architecture under Hudson/Smith’s intent-and-effects framework. Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on the MVRA’s integration into the criminal judgment and its criminal enforcement mechanisms underscores why labeling it “civil” would be both doctrinally unnatural and practically destabilizing in adjacent sentencing and procedural contexts. Justice Barrett’s point that Hudson requires us to start with statutory construction reinforces a narrow, institutionally careful holding: MVRA restitution counts as “punishment” for Ex Post Facto purposes, while leaving for remand whether the particular retroactive change actually increases punishment under Weaver. Nothing raised by colleagues suggests a principle that would coherently treat this sentencing-embedded, mandatory deprivation as nonpunitive for ex post facto analysis without generating broader instability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that restitution is “primarily remedial” under Paroline and Dolan, but that purpose-oriented description cannot displace Hudson’s threshold inquiry into Congress’s design: the MVRA directs restitution be imposed “when sentencing a defendant convicted” and “in addition to … any other penalty,” which textually situates it within the criminal sentence. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the obligation is conviction-triggered and enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms, which strongly indicates a penal sanction even if it also compensates victims. Justice Alito’s workability concerns reinforce the statutory-reading point: recharacterizing MVRA restitution as purely civil would create doctrinal instability (including Seventh Amendment and sentencing-procedure spillover) that suggests Congress did not create a freestanding civil damages remedy. I would therefore hold MVRA restitution is “punishment” for Ex Post Facto classification and, consistent with the narrow course Roberts outlines, leave for remand whether the retroactive change increases punishment under Weaver.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that MVRA restitution is fundamentally compensatory and therefore “civil”—still doesn’t square with Congress’s design choices: restitution is conviction-triggered, mandatory, imposed “when sentencing,” and integrated into the criminal judgment and enforcement scheme, which are classic markers of penal sanction under Hudson/Smith absent the “clearest proof” to the contrary. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about the procedural and structural anomalies that would follow from reclassifying sentencing restitution as civil (including Seventh Amendment and broader sentencing-doctrine destabilization) is especially persuasive to me as a pragmatic matter focused on workability and constitutional coherence. Justice Kagan’s emphasis that Hudson begins with statutory construction reinforces that we should take Congress at its word in situating restitution within the criminal sentence, even if it also serves compensatory ends. I therefore remain with Petitioner, while agreeing that the separate question whether the retroactive change actually “increases punishment” can be left for remand under Weaver.

John Roberts.reasoning: MVRA restitution is imposed only “in addition to … any other penalty” upon conviction and is ordered as part of the criminal judgment at sentencing, 18 U.S.C. § 3663A(a)(1), which strongly indicates Congress treated it as a component of the criminal sentence rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Under this Court’s civil-versus-punitive framework (Smith v. Doe’s intent-and-effects inquiry, informed by the Mendoza-Martinez factors), the MVRA’s mandatory, conviction-triggered, court-ordered deprivation of property—enforced through criminal-sentence collection mechanisms—carries significant punitive effects even if it also compensates victims. Our restitution cases describing a “primary purpose” as remedial (e.g., Paroline; Dolan) do not overcome the MVRA’s placement and operation within the sentencing process, nor do they justify a rule that would invite destabilizing Seventh Amendment consequences by recharacterizing sentencing restitution as “civil.” A narrow disposition is appropriate: hold that MVRA restitution is “punishment” for Ex Post Facto purposes, and leave to remand whether the particular retroactive change at issue “increases punishment” within the meaning of Weaver v. Graham.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause forbids retroactive increases in criminal punishment, and the MVRA’s text and structure make restitution a component of the criminal sentence: it is imposed only “when sentencing a defendant convicted of” specified crimes and must be ordered “in addition to … any other penalty,” 18 U.S.C. § 3663A(a)(1). Under this Court’s intent-effects framework (Smith v. Doe; Mendoza-Martinez), Congress’ evident choice to embed restitution in the sentencing judgment and to enforce it through criminal-judgment mechanisms confirms punitive intent; at a minimum, restitution is a sanction “by reason of” conviction rather than a freestanding civil remedy (cf. United States v. Ursery’s emphasis on Congress’ designation and procedural setting). Precedents describing restitution as “primarily” remedial (e.g., Dolan; Paroline) do not control the constitutional classification where the statute mandates a conviction-triggered deprivation as part of the judgment of sentence. Because MVRA restitution is punishment, its retroactive application that disadvantages the defendant triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause, leaving any dispute about whether a particular amendment increases punishment for remand.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Restitution under the MVRA, 18 U.S.C. § 3663A, is imposed only upon conviction and as part of the sentencing process, and it is enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms, which strongly indicates it operates as a component of the criminal sentence rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Even under the intent-effects framework described in Smith v. Doe, Congress placed restitution within the criminal code and tethered it to conviction and sentencing, and the measure’s operation is sufficiently punitive in form and effect to trigger Ex Post Facto scrutiny when applied retroactively. This conclusion also avoids the serious practical and structural consequences of recharacterizing MVRA restitution as “civil,” including destabilizing settled Sixth/Seventh Amendment treatment of restitution determinations referenced in cases like Apprendi and Feltner. Because the question presented is classification, not whether a specific retroactive change “increases punishment,” I would hold MVRA restitution is punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes and vacate for further proceedings on any remaining increase-in-punishment issue.

Under Smith v. Doe’s two-step inquiry, whatever Congress’s compensatory rhetoric, the MVRA’s mandatory, court-ordered, conviction-triggered scheme—serving deterrent and rehabilitative aims described in cases like Paroline and Dolan—has sufficiently punitive form and effect to qualify as “punishment” for Ex Post Facto purposes. Treating restitution as “civil” would also risk undermining settled sentencing practice and create serious constitutional dislocation (including the jury-trial implications highlighted by Tull and Feltner) by recharacterizing core sentencing determinations as civil damages. Because the Ex Post Facto Clause forbids retroactive increases in criminal punishment, retroactive application of MVRA restitution provisions must be scrutinized as punishment even if some enforcement changes might not ultimately increase the penalty on remand.

United States, the inquiry is “at least initially” one of statutory construction, and here Congress situated restitution in the criminal code and tethered it to sentencing, which is strong evidence it is penal in nature notwithstanding its compensatory aim.
